zebralogic.title: Consolidate Direct Equivalences
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly equates two or more attribute values, merge them into a single composite fact and propagate that fact throughout the puzzle. Without this, the solver may treat the linked attributes as independent, leading to contradictory placements.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue states that two (or more) attributes refer to the same house (e.g., "X is Y", "X's Y is Z").
zebralogic.example: Treating "Birthday May" and "Food spaghetti" as unrelated and assigning them to different houses.

zebralogic.title: Assign Fixed Positions Immediately
zebralogic.principle: If a clue pins an attribute to a specific house number, place that attribute (and any directly linked attributes) in that house right away. Delaying this placement wastes constraints and can cause later contradictions.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says "X is in house N" or provides a direct positional relationship that fixes a house number.
zebralogic.example: Leaving "Eric" unassigned despite the clue that he occupies house 3, later causing an impossible configuration.

zebralogic.title: Translate 'N houses between' to Exact Distance
zebralogic.principle: A clue that says "exactly N houses between X and Y" means the positions of X and Y differ by N+1 houses. Converting the wording to a numeric distance prevents off‑by‑one errors.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses the phrase "exactly N houses between" (or equivalent wording).
zebralogic.example: Placing X and Y adjacent when the clue required one house between them.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Adjacency for 'next to' and Ordered Left
zebralogic.principle: Adjacency clues ('next to', 'directly left of', 'directly right of') impose a distance of one house and a direction. Ignoring the distance or direction leads to misplaced items.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses "next to", "directly left of", or "directly right of".
zebralogic.example: Treating "Peter is directly left of Alice" as merely "Peter is somewhere left of Alice" and not enforcing adjacency.

zebralogic.title: Output Solution in Expected JSON Table Format
zebralogic.principle: The verifier expects a JSON object with a "header" array and a "rows" array; any deviation (e.g., plain text, missing fields) causes rejection even if the grid is correct.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: At the very end of the response, before sending it to the verifier.
zebralogic.example: Returning a formatted table without the surrounding JSON wrapper.

zebralogic.title: Keep Reasoning Concise to Avoid Token Truncation
zebralogic.principle: The model has a token budget; excessive reasoning can truncate the final JSON, making the answer invalid. Keep explanatory text short enough to leave sufficient tokens for the complete solution.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: During solution generation, before emitting the final JSON.
zebralogic.example: Including a long narrative that pushes the JSON beyond the token limit, resulting in a cut‑off answer.

zebralogic.title: Preserve Original Attribute Tokens (Case and Spelling)
zebralogic.principle: Attribute values must be reproduced exactly as given (including case, spaces, punctuation). Any deviation causes a mismatch with the reference solution.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When writing the final JSON rows.
zebralogic.example: Writing "OnePlus 9" instead of the exact token "oneplus 9" from the attribute list.

zebralogic.title: Directional Ordering for 'somewhere to the left/right of' constraints
zebralogic.principle: Clues that say "X is somewhere to the left/right of Y" impose a strict ordering (X < Y or X > Y) but not adjacency. Treat them as ordering constraints, not distance constraints.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses "somewhere to the left of" or "somewhere to the right of".
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "X is somewhere to the left of Y" as requiring X to be directly left of Y.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Exclusion Constraints for Specific House Numbers
zebralogic.principle: If a clue forbids an attribute from a particular house, remove that house from its domain immediately. Ignoring exclusions can lead to impossible placements.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says "X is not in house N" or similar.
zebralogic.example: Allowing Peter to be placed in house 5 despite the clue that he is not.

zebralogic.title: Transitive Ordering Inference
zebralogic.principle: When multiple direct ordering clues form a chain, infer the implied indirect orderings (e.g., A left of B and B left of C implies A left of C). Missing transitive inference leaves the search space larger.
zebralogic.example: Knowing A left of B and B left of C but failing to deduce that A must be left of C.

zebralogic.description: Generating overly long reasoning before the final answer, causing token truncation.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model exceeds its token budget, so the tail of the output (including the JSON) gets cut off.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Limit explanatory text and reserve enough tokens for the complete JSON solution.

zebralogic.description: Providing the solution in a format not recognized by the verifier.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The output does not match the expected JSON schema (e.g., missing header, using plain text).
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Always output a JSON object with a "header" array and a "rows" array as specified.

zebralogic.description: Using incorrect case or synonyms for attribute values.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: Attribute tokens are reproduced from memory instead of copied verbatim, causing mismatches.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute values exactly as they appear in the problem statement, preserving case, spacing, and punctuation.

zebralogic.description: Misinterpreting adjacency constraints that involve a named entity and a non‑name attribute, treating them as non‑adjacent or placing both in the same house.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The solver treats the named entity and the attribute as separate categories and forgets that adjacency applies to houses, not attribute types.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Apply adjacency rules uniformly, regardless of whether the items are names, foods, pets, etc.; enforce a distance of one house between them.
